source: Pati, Li, Jha, Garg, Sejpal, Ganesh (2026) MathConstraint: Automated Generation of Verified Combinatorial Reasoning Instances for LLMs
finding: First 2026 head-to-head of reasoning-capable frontier models with and without a sandboxed Python tool that has pysat/z3/pycosat. Tools help a lot even for models that think. Gap 1.
numbers: 329 hard SAT/UNSAT-style instances, 8 tool rounds, temp 0, max 16,384 tokens. No tools -> tools: GPT-5.5 66.9 -> 80.9; Claude-Opus-4.7 42.6 -> 77.5; Claude-4.6-Sonnet 18.5 -> 70.5; Gemini-3.1-Pro 51.7 -> 72.9; Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite 24.9 -> 62.3; Grok-4.20 58.1 -> 66.6. Mean gain +28 pp over 12 models. Only 3 of 12 models above 50% without tools. Easy split (266): tools approach saturation near 90%.
quote: Tool access roughly doubles frontier accuracy on MATHCONSTRAINT (mean +28pp
limits: Reasoning settings differ per model: discrete effort at max for models that expose it, Opus thinking budget 8k, Sonnet no thinking budget, others none. So the biggest gain (Sonnet) is a non-thinking model. Token budgets are not equal. Answers are SAT/UNSAT claims plus a code-checked witness, not a classic logic puzzle. Solver choice is left to the model.
agent_relevance: Even the strongest reasoning model (GPT-5.5, max effort) gains 14 pp from a code sandbox. Supports a code-run S4/S7 step for combinatorial items, but the gain is smaller for models that already think long.

source: Pati et al. (2026) MathConstraint, efficiency tables 12 and 13
finding: Tool use did not cost more tokens for the strongest thinking models and cut dollars per instance. For non-thinking or small models tokens grew. First published per-instance cost with and without a solver tool on the same items. Gap 2.
limits: Not an equal-token curve: each model used its own length. Cost includes price differences per model. Some rows in the PDF text dump had shifted columns; only rows that aligned are quoted. The reasoning-only baseline was not given a bigger budget.
agent_relevance: A solver call can replace a long thinking trace. The honest comparison for our agent is accuracy at matched total tokens; this paper gives per-model points but not curves, so gap 2 is only partly closed.

source: Pati et al. (2026) MathConstraint, SIM@k tool-budget replay (Table 11, section 4.3)
finding: Solver-tool accuracy depends strongly on how many tool rounds are allowed. Most successful runs are multi-round (write, debug, run, submit), not one solver call. Gaps 2 and 5.
numbers: SIM@1 / @2 / @4 / @8 (accuracy %): GPT-5.5 19.5 / 41.0 / 63.2 / 80.9; Claude-Opus-4.7 3.3 / 30.4 / 59.3 / 77.5; Claude-4.6-Sonnet 0.0 / 6.1 / 33.7 / 70.5; Gemini-3.1-Pro 0.9 / 18.2 / 50.2 / 72.9; Grok-4.20 7.9 / 28.0 / 45.3 / 66.6. Halving 8 to 4 rounds costs up to 37 pp. Force-submit rescue: GPT-5.5 passes 67 of 88 force-submitted traces (76.1%), DeepSeek-V4-Flash 19 of 180 (10.6%).
limits: SIM@k truncates logged traces; the authors call it a conservative lower bound because a model told the budget might plan better. Single run, temperature 0.
agent_relevance: Retry and repair rounds are where the accuracy comes from. A spec-then-solve loop needs a round budget of about 4 to 8 and a rule for what to do when the budget ends.

source: Pati et al. (2026) MathConstraint, witness gap and free-UNSAT baseline (section 4.1, Tables 2, 4)
finding: Without tools, models say SAT but cannot produce a witness that survives exact code verification. The verifier requires a concrete witness, so tools shrink but do not remove the SAT-bias gap. Gap 8.
numbers: No tools, SAT-claim accuracy minus verified accuracy: Llama-3.3-70B +54.4 pp, Claude-4.6-Sonnet +53.5 pp (72.0 vs 18.5), Gemini-Flash-Lite +51.4 pp, GPT-5.5 +12.1 pp (79.0 vs 66.9, my subtraction). With tools: Sonnet SAT-claim 91.8 vs verified 70.5 (gap 21.3, my subtraction), GPT-5.5 94.2 vs 80.9 (gap 13.3, my subtraction). 30.7% of items are UNSAT; Sonnet gets only 16.8% on UNSAT without tools, Llama 24.8%.
quote: Deciding existence is easier than constructing an object that survives exact verification.
limits: The SAT Acc column is defined in the paper's appendix; gaps other than the three quoted were derived by me from Tables 2 and 4. Not an A/B of witness-required vs not: the verifier always requires a witness, so the intervention is built in, not tested.
agent_relevance: A code verifier on the witness turns silent SAT-bias into a visible failure (the answer is marked wrong and the agent can retry). It does not make models right: 13 to 21 pp remain even with tools.

source: Pati et al. (2026) MathConstraint, solver time as difficulty probe (section 4.4)
finding: Solver wall time separates easy and hard releases, but within the hard release it does not predict which instances LLMs fail. Gap 10 (negative).
numbers: Median reference solver time 0.20 s (easy) vs 2.52 s (hard); p99 11.8 s vs 653 s. Within the hard release, log solver time correlates -0.15 with no-tools cross-model accuracy and -0.14 with tool-enabled accuracy; accuracy is roughly flat across solver-time quartiles. Frontier no-tools accuracy 72.6-87.6% (easy) vs 18.5-66.9% (hard).
quote: ranking individual natural-language instances by LLM difficulty requires features that solver wall time alone does not expose
limits: Mixed problem families (pysms extremal graphs vs pycsp). Correlation over model means, 329 items. Not a test of Z3 conflict count specifically.
agent_relevance: A solver-side hardness number alone is not enough to set a per-item token budget. Combine with model-side signals such as first-try verifier failure.

source: Pati et al. (2026) MathConstraint, tool fingerprints and backend asymmetry (sections 4.1, 4.2, Table 20)
finding: Models differ in what they write when given a Python sandbox. Z3 is not the default for most. Gap 7 (partial).
numbers: Share of execute_python calls: Grok-4.20 uses z3 in 44%; Gemini-3.1-Pro pysat 32% and z3 26%; Claude Sonnet 60% and Opus 54% brute-force loops (pysat second); Llama-3.3-70B networkx 50%. No-tools mean accuracy by backend: 61.1% on pysms (extremal graphs) vs 29.0% on pycsp (unique numeric objects); frontier cohort 66.5 vs 33.6.
limits: Models chose the library themselves; no forced-language comparison. Accuracy by language is not reported, only usage share. No Z3Py-only arm.
agent_relevance: Do not assume the model will reach for Z3. If we want a solver, the scaffold must name it and show one example. Brute-force code is a valid fallback for small domains.

source: Kesseli, O'Hearn, Cabral (2025) Logic.py: Bridging the Gap between LLMs and Constraint Solvers
finding: A Llama-3.1-70B model writing puzzles in a small Python-like constraint language (Logic.py), solved by a constraint solver, beat o1-preview on ZebraLogicBench. Gap 1 (older reasoning model).
numbers: ZebraLogicBench puzzle accuracy: Logic Agent 91.4 (easy 97.86, hard 88.89) vs o1-preview 71.4 (98.57, 60.83), o1-mini 59.7, Claude-3.5-Sonnet 36.2, GPT-4o 31.7. Base Llama-3.1-70B alone 24.9 (easy 73.57, hard 5.97). Cell accuracy o1-preview 92.98.
quote: setting a new state-of-the-art with an accuracy of over 90%
limits: o1-preview is the only reasoning model; no o3, R1, GPT-5. No token or cost comparison. Authors say the DSL prototype is incomplete and the result may not carry to other search problems. Narrow puzzle family. Baseline numbers come from the public leaderboard, not rerun.
agent_relevance: A cheap model with a solver beat the best thinking model of late 2024 by 20 points overall and 28 on hard grids. Needs a retest with 2025-26 reasoning models.

source: He and Wang (2025) When Do Symbolic Solvers Enhance Reasoning in Large Language Models?
finding: Solver-style code helps when the task is a constraint search with little implicit reasoning, and hurts on commonsense-heavy text. Declarative one-shot beats zero-shot. Python has fewer syntax errors than Prolog. Gaps 4 and 7.
numbers: GPT-4o, greedy, up to 10 retries. ZebraLogic easy/hard/avg: CoT 77.9/8.9/28.2; Prolog zero-shot 64.6/15.0/28.9; Prolog declarative one-shot 96.8/44.0/58.8; Python zero-shot 69.7/26.5/38.1; Python declarative one-shot 96.4/62.1/71.7. CodeLlama-13B Python one-shot 62.5/14.6/28.5. EntailmentBank: CoT 81.8 vs Prolog zero-shot 27.4. GSM8K: CoT 94.6 vs Prolog zero-shot 85.8. 4x4 grids: Claude-3.5 10.0 (3x3 62.5) vs GPT-4o with code 72.5 (3x3 90).
quote: symbolic-solver-integrated methods may fail to capture the implicit rules in certain problems
limits: Solvers are SymPy and clpr, not Z3. GPT-4o and CodeLlama only; no reasoning model was run although the paper is motivated by overthinking. Table text was garbled in the PDF dump; rows matched by prompt labels. Retries: ZebraLogic Python one-shot 84% at 1 try and 84% at 10, so retries fix syntax, not wrong specs.
agent_relevance: Gives the only measured wrong-routing cost I found: a fuzzy task (EntailmentBank) sent down the Prolog path loses 54 points vs CoT; a hard grid sent down CoT loses 50+ points vs Python. Python beats Prolog; no Z3Py comparison.

source: Lin et al. (2025) ZebraLogic: On the Scaling Limits of LLMs for Logical Reasoning, best-of-N and self-verify rows
finding: Re-read of the best-of-N table for gap 6: no code checker is used anywhere; the oracle is the ground-truth answer. Nothing closes the oracle gap with a real checker.
numbers: GPT-4o overall: greedy 31.7; BoN-Oracle N=32 60.3, N=128 69.1; majority vote N=32 38.0 (N=128 37.6); BoN reward model N=32 34.8; Self-Verify about 32 to 34 (oracle variant 33.0). X-large: oracle N=32 7.0, majority 2.5, reward model 0.0, greedy 0.5.
limits: Row labels in the PDF text were shifted; values above are the rows I could align. A clue checker needs the clues turned into code, which is the same hard translation step.
agent_relevance: The oracle gap (60-69 vs 38) is the upper bound a clue-checking code picker could reach. Nobody has written that checker in a paper. Gap 6 stays open.

source: Lin et al. (2025) ZebraLogic, hidden reasoning tokens (section 6.1, Figure 4)
finding: Per-instance token cost of the reasoning-only baseline on grid puzzles, useful as the denominator for any equal-token comparison. Gap 2.
numbers: Mean hidden reasoning tokens: o1-mini 5,144.6, o1-preview 5,346.3, vs GPT-4o-mini 502.9 and GPT-4o 543.7. Below 20 Z3 conflicts about 400 hidden tokens per conflict; flat above about 30.
limits: OpenAI o1 era (2024). No data for R1, o3, GPT-5.
agent_relevance: On grid puzzles a thinking model spends about 5k tokens; a spec plus solver run must beat that. MathConstraint shows tool runs cost 12k to 35k tokens on a harder set, so equality is not obvious.

source: Wei et al. (2025) SATBench, error analysis and error-aware prompting (sections 5.3, 6.2)
finding: SAT-bias is the main failure of reasoning models on SAT-derived puzzles, and a prompt-only reminder fixes about two thirds of failing cases. No code checker was tried. Gap 8.
numbers: Share of errors: Satisfiability Bias o4-mini 68.7%, DeepSeek-R1 40.5%; Context Inconsistency 17.0% / 44.7%; Condition Omission 14.3% / 12.6%; Spurious Priors 0.0% / 2.1%. Error-aware prompts corrected 60.4% of failing cases for o4-mini and 73.2% for R1. Prediction vs trace accuracy: o4-mini SAT 94.7 vs 74.6; Claude-3.7 83.2 vs 47.4.
quote: models often show a bias toward predicting SAT outcomes without a valid variable assignment
limits: Error classes were assigned on a sample (size not recorded in my read). The correction rate is measured on the failing cases that shaped the prompt, with no held-out set. No assignment-verifier arm.
agent_relevance: A reminder 'if you answer SAT, list the assignment and check each clause' is a no-cost S4 step; a code check of the assignment is the stronger version and is untested.

source: Wei et al. (2025) SATBench, human validation of formalisation and narrative vs formula (section 5.4, Table 6)
finding: Measures how often the clause-to-text translation is wrong and how much the text wrapper costs. Closest hard number for gap 3, but it is the story-generation direction, not model-written specs. Gap 9: hardness varied by clause count only.
numbers: Human check: clause translation faithfulness 97% (three minor errors); scenario and mapping consistency 100%; judge correctness 93%. Narrative puzzle vs raw CNF accuracy: GPT-4o-mini 53.6 vs 54.8; GPT-4o 58.2 vs 59.2; DeepSeek-V3 84.0 vs 87.3; o4-mini 89.4 vs 94.3. No clause-to-variable ratio sweep (Figure 4 uses clause count).
limits: Direction is formula to text, the reverse of what an agent does. Three co-author annotators; sample size not recorded in my read.
agent_relevance: Even a pipeline that starts from the formula garbles about 3 in 100 clauses. Text-to-formula by a model should be expected to do worse; verify it by round trip.

source: Feng, Weir, Bostrom et al. (2025) VeriCoT: Neuro-Symbolic Chain-of-Thought Validation via Logical Consistency Checks
finding: Each CoT step is translated to SMT-LIB and checked for entailment from stated and inferred premises. The authors state that a wrong translation cannot be detected by the solver. Gap 3 (stays open).
numbers: Self-reflection on VeriCoT feedback: average +12.3 pp absolute (46.4% relative) verification pass rate and +9.5 pp (41.1% relative) verified-correct-answer rate across ProofWriter, BioASQ, LegalBench-SARA. DPO on verified traces: pass rate +4.3 pp (18.4% relative). LLM-as-judge premise acceptability 77.0 to 96.4 by dataset and premise type.
quote: it cannot guarantee that the NL CoT or the premises are correct
limits: Tables extracted garbled; per-dataset precision not relied on. Pass rate measures consistency, not match with the original text. Premises are model-made.
agent_relevance: Confirms the silent-translation risk is known and unsolved: consistency checks pass when the formula is wrong but self-consistent. Needs an independent check such as round trip or a second translation.

source: Ganguly, Iyengar et al. (2024) Proof of Thought, StrategyQA run
finding: Re-opened. A fixed JSON-to-Z3 pipeline on a fuzzy commonsense set compiles most programs but has poor precision, so compile success does not signal fit. Gap 4 (cost of wrong routing).
numbers: 1000 StrategyQA questions, initial prompt plus 2 repair attempts: 82.4% of programs compiled and ran; precision 58.22%; false-positive rate 53.98%; balanced score 71.13 as reported.
limits: No same-sample CoT comparison in my read. Authors present it as room for improvement.
agent_relevance: A compile-success gate is not a crispness gate: 82% compiled while 54% of negatives were called positive. Use agreement with a plain baseline answer instead.

source: Kambhampati et al. (2024) LLMs Can't Plan, But Can Help Planning in LLM-Modulo Frameworks
finding: Primary source for the generate-test loop with external critics. The 20% and 65% figures quoted second-hand in earlier notes are not in this paper; it cites other papers' results. Gaps 5 and 6.
numbers: About 12% of LLM plans are executable in the cited work. Citing Valmeekam et al.: with VAL back-prompting, Blocks World reaches 82% within 15 rounds, Logistics 70%, obfuscated Mystery Blocks World about 10%. Travel planning: critics in the loop give 6x baseline within 10 rounds; benchmark authors' best GPT-3.5 strategy 0.7%.
limits: Position paper citing companion papers; not run here. The 20%/65% could not be matched.
agent_relevance: A verifier loop works only when the generator can propose plausible candidates (Mystery BW stays near 10%). The same limit should apply to spec-writing.
